records.table: Canadian Club 1858 Original is the blended Canadian whisky made at Windsor, Ontario, across the river from Detroit, where Hiram Walker set up his distillery. Almond, light pepper and vanilla over a dry finish: pour it long with ginger ale or soda.
records.story: Hiram Walker (1816 to 1899), a grocer and grain merchant from Massachusetts, turned to distilling in Detroit in the 1850s. Michigan's temperance laws pressed on the trade, and he bought land across the river in what is now Ontario, where a distillery and flour mill were soon at work; the house dates its beginning to 1858, and the town that grew round the works was called Walkerville. His whisky found a following in the gentlemen's clubs of the United States and came to be known as Club Whisky. American distillers then pressed for imported whisky to name its country of origin, and the word Canadian went onto the label. When the United States went dry in January 1920, Ontario went on letting its distillers make whisky for export, and Windsor, facing Detroit across the water, became a smugglers' crossing: by the brand's account Canadian Club was run across the border and counterfeited by bootleggers. The whisky is made at Windsor, on the site Walker chose. For a bartender it is the Canadian whisky a guest names in a highball, and the bottle that shows what a light Canadian blend does with ginger ale.

records.story: In the spring of 1939 King George VI and Queen Elizabeth crossed Canada by train, the first time, as the Canadian Encyclopedia tells it, that a reigning monarch had set foot in the country. Seagram, the Canadian distiller, made a whisky for the tour under its president. By the brand's account some six hundred blends were tried before one of about fifty whiskies was chosen; it went into a cut-glass bottle and a purple bag stitched in gold, and ten cases rode the royal train. For years it was sold only in Canada, and it crossed into the United States in the 1960s. The making came to rest at Gimli, a town on the western shore of Lake Winnipeg in Manitoba, where column stills of many sizes make the base and flavouring whiskies the blenders marry. In 2000 Seagram was sold to Vivendi, whose drinks were then divided between Diageo and Pernod Ricard, and Crown Royal went to Diageo. For a bartender it is the Canadian whisky many a guest asks for by its purple bag, and the plain lesson in what a blend of many component whiskies means.

records.story: The house dates its whisky to 1857, when the man whose name the label carries came to Prescott, a town on the St. Lawrence River in eastern Ontario, to run a distillery there, as its manager by most accounts and as a partner by one, and the whisky came to carry his name and his initials. After his death the business passed from his heirs: in 1918, by most accounts, a new holding company that had taken in the Corby distillery at Corbyville, near Belleville, bought it, and the making left Prescott for Corbyville. In 1989 the Corbyville distillery closed after 132 years, and its maturing whisky went to the Hiram Walker distillery in Windsor, where Wiser's is distilled and bottled. Deluxe is the everyday blend of the range: corn for a light body and rye for spice, married by the blenders. Around it the house built older bottlings, rye-led ones and blends of great age. For a bartender it is the plain Ontario lesson in how Canadian whisky is assembled from component whiskies, and the bottle to pour when a guest wants a soft Canadian with ginger ale.

records.story: The distillery at Grimsby, on the Niagara shore of Lake Ontario, began, by the house's account, in 1972, when it was opened to make fruit brandies. In 1992 a winemaker bought it, renamed it Kittling Ridge and made wine and spirits there, with a blender beside him from the start. The whisky grew from his own trials: instead of mashing the grains together and ageing the spirit as one, he distilled corn, rye and barley each on its own and aged each apart, then blended the finished whiskies. Barrel Select, first released in 2000, was the result, and the house calls it its flagship. The label's name came to stand for the place, and in 2012 the distillery took the name Forty Creek. New bottlings followed, among them Copper Pot, later renamed Copper Bold, and Double Barrel Reserve. For a bartender Barrel Select is the bottle of the newer Ontario school: a blend of grain whiskies made apart, the way a winemaker keeps separate lots, and a Canadian to set beside the older houses of Windsor.

records.story: The name looks back to 1784, when, at the end of the American war, a settler took land at Ernestown, near Lake Ontario, and came to keep grist mills, one of them on a plot known as Lot 40. Two centuries on, a descendant of his, then master distiller at Hiram Walker in Windsor, made a whisky in his memory: rye in a pot still, as he supposed early Canadian distillers made it. It came out in 1998, one of three whiskies the distillery released together under a single banner, but within a few years it was gone from the shelves. In 2012 the Windsor blenders brought it back, distilled in a single copper pot still and aged in virgin oak. Around the revived whisky grew a family of bottlings: Dark Oak, cask strength editions and finishes in other woods. For a bartender it answers a question the style raises at the table: the Canadian word rye promises no rye share, and here the whole mash is rye.

open: bottle.mash: whether today's bottle is all unmalted rye rests on the importer alone; one shop gives 10 per cent malted barley.

bottle.name: the label's words differ by market (Canadian Rye Whisky in US listings, Single Copper Pot Still Canadian Whisky in Ontario, 100% Pot Still Rye Whisky on the house's shop); the roster's name stands.
bottle.wood: virgin white oak on Corby's and Pernod Ricard's pages, new charred American oak on the house shop; the char of the standard bottling was not found.
